Tech Report: Men of Pause: Redefining Manhood Through Vasectomy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1104 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • Sources indicate that december 2014.
  • Sources indicate that she wasn't asking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

Co-authored with Galit Romanelli.

Galit said it in the recovery room.

Sources indicate that december 2014. She had just come out of an emergency C-section with our daughter. She was still shaking on the recovery table. She looked at me and remarked: “I'm done.”.

Sources indicate that she wasn't asking. She wasn't pushing me. She was just done.

It has been revealed that september 2019. Galit needed to replace her IUD. This time, for the first time, we actually had an open discussion about it. Why does she need to take sole responsibility for birth control for both of us? I started considering a vasectomy. But I was scared. Not of the procedure. Scared of what it meant. Scared to close that chapter. Scared to end the part of me that was still, biologically, a man with options.

Sources indicate that we researched, met a urologist, but ultimately, at the last minute, I bailed. Galit was happy that at least we spoke about it openly.

February 2026. I finally had my vasectomy.

Recent findings suggest that the first time someone cut that part of my body, I was eight days old. I didn't choose it. I was ushered into a covenant, a tradition. This happened before I could speak, before I could consent, before I even knew I had a body.

Recent findings suggest that that is how it goes for most men. The first major act performed on our reproductive organ happens without our permission. We enter the tribe like everyone else. Unaware. Another boy marked into the tribe.

Sources indicate that for many of us, that pattern continues. Sex gets socialized into us as performance, as conquest, as something we take. Reproduction becomes the measure of our masculinity. Our job is to spread our seed. We are procreators. That is our identity. So when the vasectomy conversation comes up, most men hear one thing: Loss. That’s how I felt back then.

I want to suggest the opposite: A vasectomy doesn’t hurt your masculinity, it actually liberates you.

Some men hear the word vasectomy and their stomach tightens. It sounds like castration. Like a punishment.

It has been revealed that I understand that feeling. Anything that touches that part of us is triggering. That part is the symbol for what we learn is our worth, our trophy, our uniqueness. Limiting or “damaging” it threatens our sense of manhood.

But this is different. This time you have agency. This is a choice you make. You decide what happens to your body. Not your parents. Not your religion.

It has been revealed that in a way, vasectomy is a form of positive liberty. The first circumcision wasn’t your choice. Someone chose for you. The second one was made of your free choice. You choose it because you want to.

Isaiah Berlin called this positive liberty. By choosing the second cut, you gain the (positive) freedom to live your life according to your values.

Here’s what I didn’t expect. It’s been about 9 months since the operation and nothing has changed. Not physically. Not sexually. Not sensually. To be honest, my body feels like the procedure never happened.

The only thing that changed is how I see myself.

It was a symbolic circumcision. A symbolic change.

According to recent reports, maybe I'm entering another tribe now. A tribe of older men who are ready to initiate others, because it is no longer about me.

According to recent reports, this is the threshold we wrote about in the relational hero's journey. Once he crosses the point of no return, he embarks on a journey, which will change him forever. He will return ‘home’, a wiser hero, bringing his latest wisdom and abilities to change the world.

According to recent reports, this is also what middle age has been teaching me. The focus shifts. From spreading the seed to serving others. From building my own life to initiating the men coming up behind me. Guiding men into mature, differentiated manhood. The books Iron John and The New Manhood teach us that the older man's task is not to keep proving himself. It is to initiate the younger ones. To age and to sage. A vasectomy, for me, was one way of stepping into that.

I call this being a man of pause. To pause, reflect, and take the time to care for others.

There is a principle screenwriting teacher Robert McKee returns to. The artist becomes more creative inside their limitation not outside it. I have felt this everywhere. Writing a PhD inside its rules. Training for a marathon within the proposal. Learning to touch my wife the way she wants in a 30-day challenge. The limit is what helped me be better.

Industry observers note that the vasectomy is a creative limitation. I blocked one dimension of my sexuality, the reproductive one, and what I got back was focus. Energy that is no longer worried about an unwanted pregnancy. Energy I can channel somewhere else. Toward my marriage, my art, my clinical work. Toward changing the world in the years I have left.

We fixate on what we will not be able to do anymore. The better question is what this limitation will open up? When you close the door on your reproduction, what new vista will appear?

It has been revealed that I am not telling you to get a vasectomy. That is between you and your partner. I am asking you something else. I'm asking you to ask yourself:.

Where in your life are you willing to cut something off?

Where are you ready to limit yourself?

Where do you dare to block one dimension of you, so you can evolve into the next version of yourself?

Where and how are you ready to evolve your manhood?

If men stopped thinking about themselves, put their ego aside, and turned toward service, that would change the world.

When you were a baby, someone made that choice for you.

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D.-candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

Tech Report: The 61 Best Fresh Reveals of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

📅 13 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, THE IDEA OF "fresh" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days.
  • But at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong.
  • Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, THE IDEA OF "fresh" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a big way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

But at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

Industry observers note that and they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the demonstrates we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (HBO).

In shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock).

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

It has been revealed that at the very least, Wonder Man is among the best reveals Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

One of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

This wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The fresh season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

Sources indicate that DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best highlights of the year.

Sources indicate that the second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

It has been revealed that one of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

It has been revealed that the erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting upcoming highlights. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

Recent findings suggest that from the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

Sources indicate that there are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

Industry observers note that sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

In a recent development, this series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of Fresh York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in highlights like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those intends have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

Jury Duty: Manufacturer Retreat (Prime Video).

It has been revealed that after striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Company Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

Sources indicate that riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix).

Camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand Fresh Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

What are those weird things on a turkey’s beak?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when a tom turkey is relaxed, the fleshy growth above his beak is short and stubby, like a little unicorn horn.
  • Richard Buchholz, a professor of biology at the University of Mississippi, is the best person to ask.
  • It has been revealed that [ Related: How did Thanksgiving turkeys get so darn big?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when a tom turkey is relaxed, the fleshy growth above his beak is short and stubby, like a little unicorn horn. But when he struts to attract mates or establish dominance, blood rushes into the growth, known as the “snood.” The snood then swells and lengthens until it drapes over the turkey’s beak like a long pink earring. Turkey hens have snoods too, but theirs are smaller. So why would a male bird grow something that looks so impractical?

Recent findings suggest that dr. Richard Buchholz, a professor of biology at the University of Mississippi, is the best person to ask. Features of bird anatomy that seem more decorative than useful, which biologists call “ornaments,” have long fascinated Buchholz. For his master’s degree, Buchholz studied the yellow-knobbed curassow, a South American bird with a bright yellow knob on its bill and a crest of curly feathers.

It has been revealed that [ Related: How did Thanksgiving turkeys get so darn big? ].

Sources indicate that when it came time to choose a PhD topic, his advisor suggested a more common bird: the wild turkey. Buchholz wasn’t keen. “I don’t wanna be the turkey guy,” he told his advisor. Still, he gave it a try. More than three decades later, he’s still studying them. And his research has shown that turkey snoods have at least two functions: seduction and status.

In a recent development, it turns out that snoods are tools of seduction. In a 1995 study by Buchholz that used both live male turkeys and decoys, females highlighted a distinct preference for males with longer snoods and wider skullcaps. (The skullcap is the smooth patch of bare skin on top of a tom’s head.).

This was surprising because male turkeys have several ornaments, including a beard that grows from their breast area, iridescent feathers, and a tail fan similar to that of a peacock. Yet females seem to care more about the snood and skullcap.

Lady turkeys are discerning birds. In some trials, females were choosing between two males whose snoods differed by “just a couple millimeters,” Buchholz notes—and they still went for the longer one.

It has been revealed that he found a likely reason for this preference in male turkeys’ guts. Males with longer snoods had fewer coccidia in their digestive tract. Coccidia are single-celled parasites that damage the lining of the intestine and can be fatal in young animals.

Buchholz thinks that snoods are indicators of health, allowing females to assess a male’s quality as a mate just by looking at them. A long snood signals a male whose immune system is strong enough to fight off parasites like coccidia, and who may pass on that disease resistance to their offspring, thus improving their chances of survival.

Another set of experiments, which Buchholz published in 1997, suggests that male turkeys also use snoods to size up the competition.

Buchholz trained captive male turkeys, each housed on its own, to enter an arena where bird seed was waiting. “They love bird seed,” Buchholz claims. “Normally, in captivity they’re fed dry pelleted food, so they love anything that looks like a natural grain or seed.”.

According to recent reports, when Buchholz let two males enter the arena at the same time, they rarely engaged in a physical fight over the treat. “Almost always, one male would give up,” Buchholz says. “The male with a longer snood typically would not be the male who gave up.”.

To check that the snood itself was what mattered, he ran the trials again with two plastic decoys that differed only in snood length. “And most of the males chose to eat the seed in front of the turkey decoy with the shorter snood of the two,” Buchholz says.

In a recent development, A turkey’s bare head and neck are covered with featherless nodules, called caruncles, which can shift in color from red or pink to white or blue. Toms have much larger caruncles than hens. “Their color can change really dramatically at different points in a male’s display,” Buchholz indicates.

But what it means is unknown. Buchholz suggests that the redness, rather than the size, could hint at anemia in the male, but admits that that’s just conjecture.

In a recent development, buchholz hasn’t directly studied the function of turkey caruncles. But as part of a 2024 study he did with Rebecca Kimball of the University of Florida, he found that bare skin helps galliform birds—a group that includes turkeys, chickens, and pheasants—to lose heat and to attract mates. So caruncles may help keep a tom cool while he catches a hen’s eye.

Sources indicate that the balancing act between body temperature regulation and courtship is the focus of Buchholz’s current research. He and his team are investigating whether rising spring temperatures affect males’ ability to display to females, and whether males choose display times and places that help them manage heat.

According to recent reports, buchholz has also made peace with his reputation. “I came to embrace the title of Turkey Man,” he says. “They’re really fascinating, socially interacting creatures.” As his research has shown, their anatomy is key to how they behave with each other. Those impractical-looking snoods are actually useful messaging tools—even if us humans might not find them as attractive as lady turkeys might.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that back in 2016, Land Rover ended production of the old-school Defender. Ineos CEO Jim Ratcliffe then entered the automotive market to fill the niche with the defiantly old-school Grenadier SUV and its pickup truck counterpart, the Quartermaster. Ineos describes the vehicles as offering “rugged British spirit and design with German engineering rigor.” And soon, the brand will add “American-made” to that mix.

Industry observers note that on Tuesday, Ineos Automotive confirmed it is moving Grenadier and Quartermaster production to the United States. The move will happen in 2028, with production moving to an undetermined location in America; an announcement on that should come within a few months. As part of the shuffle, Ineos Automotive says it will sell its current plant in Hambach, France to Chinese automaker BYD, but the brand will still build Grenadier and Quartermaster vehicles in Hambach while it sets up American facilities.

According to recent reports, “Americans have already taken the Grenadier to their hearts, and U.S. policies that have created an incredibly attractive, pro-growth business environment. Setting up production there makes so much sense. It will empower us to invest, expand, and reach even more customers around the world,” Ineos Automotive CEO Lynn Calder stated in a statement.

It has been revealed that this move should make a lot of sense for Ineos. 70 percent of the brand’s global sales are in the U.S. market, so moving production stateside would leave the brand far less exposed to American import tariffs. The Trump administration has imposed a 15 percent tariff on European Union-built vehicles, and the Quartermaster is subject to the 25 percent “chicken tax,” which dates back to the 1960s and protects the U.S. pickup truck market. Alleviating the tariff burden would allow Ineos Automotive to lower prices further, improve profit margins—or, potentially, both.

In a recent development, ineos Automotive’s announcement made no mention of the purportedly still-upcoming Fusilier, expected to launch as an EV and range-extended EV later this decade. Initial aims called for Austrian manufacturer Magna, maker of the Mercedes G-Class, to engineer and build the Fusilier at its plant in Austria.

Industry News: Does Menopausal Hormone Therapy Lower Dementia Risk? Timing and Genetics May Hold the Answer

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a latest study.
  • The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.
  • The findings could offer fresh insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a latest study.

The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.

The findings could offer fresh insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.

Researchers also found that certain associations between hormone therapy and brain health differed depending on whether women carried a genetic variant associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

Industry observers note that however, the relationship between estrogen and brain health is complex. While the findings suggest that longer estrogen exposure may be associated with healthier brain aging, they do not establish that hormone therapy can prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

The researchers drew data from the Gothenburg H70-1944 Birth Cohort, a longitudinal study of 1,203 individuals born in 1944 who resided in Gothenburg, Sweden.

The final cohort included 352 cisgender women, with an average age of 70, who had no neurological disorders and reliable self-reported data on their estrogen exposure.

Individual estrogen exposure was measured through structured interviews. It included:.

The researchers used this information as a proxy for lifetime estrogen exposure, though the study didn’t measure actual hormone levels.

Participants were also given a brain MRI at baseline and then again at a 5-year follow-up.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that those with a longer reproductive span had a lower risk of small vessel disease (SVD). Participants with a longer reproductive life span had an 8% lower risk of having two or more signs of SVD. However, later menopause, rather than earlier menstruation, appeared to be the main driver of this association.

Those who used MHT also tended to have fewer signs of SVD and better microstructural integrity in the white matter.

In individuals who carried the APOE-ε4 variant, which increases a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s disease, MHT was associated with greater cortical thickness in brain regions vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease. However, there was no association for those without this variant.

The researchers noted that longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and white matter trajectories over time.

Dung Trinh, MD, internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that estrogen has several key effects on the brain that may help support cognitive health.

It influences communication between brain cells, supports the brain’s ability to use glucose for energy, helps regulate neurotransmitters, and plays a role in maintaining healthy blood vessels and reducing inflammation and oxidative stress.

“As estrogen levels decline during menopause, some of these protective effects may diminish. Replacing estrogen closer to the menopause transition could potentially help preserve some of these functions during a vulnerable period for brain health,” he stated. “While these findings are encouraging, MHT has not been proven to prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.”.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed and noted, “Starting menopausal hormone therapy earlier in the menopause transition may help minimize some changes by supporting the brain during this period of hormonal fluctuation.”.

“There is growing interest in whether early estrogen therapy may also help reduce the long-term risk of Alzheimer’s disease, although more research is needed before we can establish that benefit,” she added.

Ross told Healthline that this research reinforces the importance of recognizing menopause as more than a reproductive or hormonal transition.

Recent findings suggest that “We know that women are disproportionately affected by dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, and some women experience noticeable cognitive changes beginning in perimenopause,” she mentioned. “If future research confirms that starting hormone therapy earlier can help protect long-term cognitive health, it could influence how we approach menopause treatment and encourage more proactive conversations between women and their healthcare providers.”.

“The goal should be to individualize treatment based on a woman’s symptoms, medical history, and overall health rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach,” Ross added.

Trinh agreed that an individualized approach to menopause management is important.

It has been revealed that “This does not mean that every woman should start hormone therapy to prevent dementia. Instead, it highlights the importance of understanding which women might benefit, when treatment should begin, and which formulations are most appropriate,” he said. “Factors such as age, time since menopause, cardiovascular risk, metabolic health, family history, and potentially genetic factors may all help guide future recommendations.”.

“We still need stronger clinical evidence before changing current prescribing guidelines specifically for dementia prevention,” Trinh added.

Tesla FSD v15 is AI4’s last shot as Musk reveals how little compute is left

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tesla’s FSD v15 is its last real shot at delivering unsupervised self-driving on the AI4 computer in millions of customer cars.
  • He also confirmed that cars won’t get the next-gen AI5 chip, and that the mid-cycle AI4.5 upgrade just had its RAM cut from 32GB to 24GB.
  • In a recent development, the most visible part of FSD v15 is Tesla Reality View, a live, video-game-like rendering of the car’s surroundings with chevrons floating in the sky for upcoming turns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tesla’s FSD v15 is its last real shot at delivering unsupervised self-driving on the AI4 computer in millions of customer cars. Elon Musk spent the weekend explaining on X how the latest software uses the hardware, and there isn’t much room left.

He also confirmed that cars won’t get the next-gen AI5 chip, and that the mid-cycle AI4.5 upgrade just had its RAM cut from 32GB to 24GB.

In a recent development, the most visible part of FSD v15 is Tesla Reality View, a live, video-game-like rendering of the car’s surroundings with chevrons floating in the sky for upcoming turns. Musk called it “real-time AI video generation (no gaming engine!) using just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator.”.

Sources indicate that the fan accounts ran with that as a flex. But Musk’s follow-up posts tell a different story.

According to recent reports, he explained that after Tesla moved a decoder into SRAM, “we only have half a TRIP out of three on SoC B, for this reality visualizer, so spent the compute as best we could.” In other words, half a TRIP is what was left over. He added that TRIP, Tesla’s neural accelerator, “basically only handles 8-bit int and has to run softmax in emulation mode in 28 steps.”.

In another post, Musk described Reality View as a roughly 1-billion-parameter diffusion model running off the same vision encoder features “that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions.” He admitted the visualization’s latency is “a bit high due to compute constraints.”.

Recent findings suggest that that 3B figure is worth noting. Tesla talked up a 10x jump in FSD model size for over a year, first for v14 and then for v15. Musk didn’t say whether 3B covers the entire driving stack, but it’s nowhere near 10x.

Sources indicate that and Tesla’s own engineers aren’t describing a chip with lots of headroom. Dilreet Raju, who works on Tesla’s AI silicon, wrote that the hardest work of his life was co-designing the v15 vision encoder “to squeeze out the last few percents of MFU from AI4.” MFU is model FLOPs utilization, a measure of how much of the chip’s theoretical compute the model actually uses. Musk replied with a target emoji.

Recent findings suggest that when Tesla unveiled its FSD computer in 2019, the selling point was redundancy: two independent chips on one board, each with its own power and memory, so one could take over if the other failed. As we noted when Tesla started shipping the AI4.5 computer in Model Y in January, Tesla’s FSD computers have historically used two identical chips for exactly that reason.

That’s what an unsupervised, Level 4 system needs. With nobody in the driver’s seat, a hardware fault can’t simply hand control back to a human. The car needs enough healthy compute left to keep seeing the road and pull over safely.

It has been revealed that but Musk’s own description shows SoC B running the decoder and the Reality View model, not sitting idle as a mirror of SoC A. Tesla hackers, including greentheonly, have reported for years that Tesla started splitting its FSD workload across both chips back in the HW3 days.

Tesla has never explained how much of AI4 it reserves for failover, or whether a single SoC can run enough of the stack to bring a car to a safe stop on its own. The more of the board v15 needs, the harder that question gets.

According to recent reports, waymo has answered it publicly. The manufacturer says both of its onboard computing systems run full workloads in parallel and that a secondary computer can bring the vehicle to a safe stop if the primary fails, backed by redundant braking, steering and power. Its fresh custom chip is rated at more than 1,000 TOPS. By our own comparison of AI4 and Nvidia’s Drive Thor, AI4 is estimated at roughly 100 to 150 TOPS across both chips.

Tesla started rolling out FSD v15 on Saturday, claiming “25x better handling of safety critical cases” without any baseline. So far, the people posting videos are mostly the usual crowd of Tesla-focused accounts that get early builds. Just hours before the rollout started, Musk wrote that v15 “goes to wide release next month.”.

It has been revealed that the early clips are almost all about Reality View, the new parking spot selection, and the floating arrows. Those are UI features. They say very little about how many miles v15 can drive between critical interventions, which is the only number that matters for unsupervised driving.

That brings us to AI4.5. On Tesla’s Q1 2026 earnings call, Musk announced an “AI4 Plus” with RAM doubled from 16GB to 32GB per chip, which raised the question of whether HW4 would follow HW3.

This weekend, Musk noted “AI4.5 is a relatively small performance improvement that is mostly due to needing to upgrade RAM to LPDDR5X.” Hours later, he added: “RAM is super expensive, so we reduced AI4.5 from 32GB to 24GB. That will be fine. It’s hard to use 32GB anyway, given memory bandwidth constraints.”.

He also mentioned that AI4 “costs twice as much now due to memory and storage price hikes.”.

It has been revealed that so the mid-cycle refresh exists mainly because Tesla needs a newer memory type it can actually buy, not to unlock bigger models. If memory bandwidth is the bottleneck, as Musk keeps repeating, adding capacity doesn’t change much.

According to recent reports, asked by an owner on Sunday whether to wait for AI5 before upgrading from HW3, Musk answered: “It’s going to Optimus. Cars will remain at AI4. That’s enough to solve superhuman driving.”.

In a recent development, an interesting comment, as it destroys one thing that HW3 owners were holding to: Tesla was delaying HW3 upgrades until it had AI5. Now, it’s clearly not the case and Tesla has no excuse not to upgrade HW3 cars.

He described AI5 as “a gigantic improvement. Roughly 12X more compute,” and later as “roughly an order of magnitude hardware performance improvement, all things considered. Memory bandwidth is a constraint.” Last year, he noted that by some metrics AI5 would be 40 times better than AI4.

Recent findings suggest that AI5 is also moving around. In October, Musk said Tesla cut AI5’s RAM in half to 72GB to get enough volume for Optimus, then nudged it back up to 96GB a day later. AI6 was cut by a third, to 144GB of LPDDR6. When asked about AI6 this weekend, Musk replied with a chef’s kiss meme.

According to recent reports, as we reported in July, Samsung’s Texas fab won’t reach AI5 volume production until the second half of 2027, nearly two years behind Musk’s original timeline. And that volume is now headed to robots and data centers, not cars.

According to recent reports, this is the situation for AI4 owners: v15 has to be the one. And we heard Elon Musk calling every FSD update “the one” for the last decade.

Sources indicate that tesla’s own engineers are talking about squeezing the last few percent of utilization out of AI4. Musk describes a half-accelerator scrap of compute left for the visualizer. The AI4.5 refresh is a RAM swap that just got downsized, and AI5 isn’t coming to cars. If v15 can’t get to unsupervised driving on AI4, there’s no hardware escape hatch for the fleet.

It has been revealed that the simple truth is that Musk doesn't know how much hardware capacity is needed for autonomous driving. Partly because Musk doesn't actually have much AI expertise. But even Tesla's engineers don't know. And they won't know until they've solved the problem. What we can say with some certainty is that as unsupervised driving is rolled out, there will be all kinds of failure modes discovered, and there's likely to be several years of continual updates the model to try to address those. Even Waymo runs into this with regularity, and they're several years ahead of Tesla on autonomy. If they're so close to exhausting AI4's capability, and their current approach is bigger and more complex models, then it seems unlikely that AI4 is going to cut it. There could always be some AI research breakthrough that enables distilling models down to smaller numbers of parameters while maintaining functionality. But Tesla doesn't really engage in that kind of pure research, so they're dependent upon someone else making the breakthrough and publishing it.

We’ve seen this movie before. Tesla said HW3 was enough for unsupervised self-driving until it wasn’t, and those owners are still waiting on an answer about upgrades. AI4 owners paid for the same promise.

And even if v15 drives well, I want to know how Tesla handles a chip failure with nobody behind the wheel. That’s not optional for Level 4. If the stack needs both SoCs to drive, what brings the car to a safe stop when one of them crashes?

It has been revealed that as for v15 itself, I’m not drawing conclusions from influencer clips. Reality View looks great, but it’s also visibly laggy, and Musk admits it’s compute-limited. A great visual update is nice. Driving performance is what matters. I’ll wait until I get it in my own car to see how big the improvement actually is.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AS LONG AS there are movies, there will be action movies.
  • In a recent development, and to the incredulity of your father (who insists no movie will ever top First Blood) the action genre hasn’t slipped on it’s roundhouse kick.
  • The only thing that’s changed are the names and faces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AS LONG AS there are movies, there will be action movies. Why? Because no young girl or boy grows up pretending to be a damsel in distress or a sidekick. They all want to punch, draw swords, and run toward the danger. They are the heroes and the future directors, choreographers, and performers who bring these imaginations to life.

In a recent development, and to the incredulity of your father (who insists no movie will ever top First Blood) the action genre hasn’t slipped on it’s roundhouse kick. If anything, we are now experiencing another golden age of ass-kicking cinema. While there are obvious developments in VFX technology, which have allowed for larger set pieces and more realistic thrills, much of what makes a great acton film a great action film hasn’t changed: painstaking choreography, fearless stunt performers/actors, and clear cinematography (and not that Taken fence jumping bullshit.).

The only thing that’s changed are the names and faces. Legend action directors like Ang Lee, John Woo, Robert Clouse, and Zhang Yimou (still going strong) have given way to newer arrivals like Gareth Evans, Chad Stahelski, and Christopher Nolan. And performers like Bruce Lee, Jean-Claude Van Damme, and Arnold have changed to Tony Jaa, Iko Uwais, and Charlize Theron.

Industry observers note that if anything, the fights are becoming more brutal, more carefully choreographed, and more ambitious. And international actors and directors are finally getting increased attention (and direction) in a Hollywood overly-saturated with slapstick cinematography and post-production punches.

Here’s hoping for more John Wicks, more Raids, and more Atomic Blondes in the future. Until then, here is, in no particular order, the 36 best action movies ever made.

John Rambo would become increasingly cartoonish as the sequels went on, but in the original, he was just a scared veteran trying to survive out in the real world.

In a recent development, the Raid was more frenzied, but the sequel (also written and directed by Gareth Evans) got grand, introducing an intricate crime-drama plot. Didn’t matter: Redemption is brilliantly violent, a ballet of broken bones, perfect punches and crazy car chases.

It has been revealed that the film marked the breakout moment for Muy Thai martial artist Tony Jaa and the beginning of one of the best action franchises ever. There’s not a lot of fakery in Jaa’s fight scenes. Dudes are getting punched for real.

The second film is more dialogue-heavy, but the first half is essentially nonstop action … and it’s a good thing the Crazy 88 fight is in black and white, because it’d almost be too bloody to watch otherwise.

Sources indicate that what should have been Jason Bourne’s final adventure is a thrilling, satisfying conclusion to this kinetic trilogy. Director Paul Greengrass and star Matt Damon permanently reshaped how we think of the globetrotting espionage thriller. James Bond is still playing catch-up.

Mission: Impossible – Rogue Nation (2015).

You can’t go wrong with any in this series – though it has only gotten better as the years have gone along – but the introduction of Rebecca Ferguson to this series just amped up the emotional stakes.

Keanu Reeves’ first of two masterful franchises on this list, John Wick gave us a mournful 21st-century assassin who won’t let his grief get in the way of shooting every bad guy in the head at point-blank range.

According to recent reports, bruce Lee was popular before this film, but this is what sent him into the stratosphere. Well-made from start to finish, and absolutely unrelenting. The best part about it is that there isn’t a gun to be found in the whole film.

In a recent development, ong-Bak gave us Tony Jaa and Muy Thai, and Ip Man gave us Donnie Yen and Wing Chun. While Yen had been in many other great action films previously (check out Kill Zone — S.P.L.), its the Ip Man films that will define his legacy, the character forever his—the semi-biographical person of Ip Man, Bruce Lee’s trainer. Though the films can feel a bit jingoistic at times (they’re basically Hong Kong’s Rambo), the fight scenes are femur-breaking legendary.

Zhang Yimou’s magnum opus, Daggers is maybe more love story than a martial arts film—and so the most action-packed love story of all time—but “love story” is no cinematic pejorative. The film features the most colorful and vibrant cinematography of any film on this list. Action is a visual genre. And no film here is more pleasing to the eyes.

Industry observers note that john Woo’s Hollywood career wasn’t as sparkling or consistent as fans would have hoped, but this late-‘80s peak remains a glorious salute to melodramatic plotting and poetic shootouts. Chow Yun-fat made for a fierce, soulful assassin — and, never forget, The Killer is where Woo began his obsession with dove-filled action scenes, which have been parodied everywhere from 21 Jump Street to Scary Movie 2.

Oh, don’t dare not think of this as an action movie. The existential dread of Ridley Scott’s original is replaced by James Cameron’s trademark intensity, and even though this has aliens and spaceship, this is as concentrated a dose of thriller mania as you will find. You’re gripping your chair just thinking about it, aren’t you?

George Miller had been mulling a fresh Mad Max film for years, and clearly, he spent that time coming up with every possible permutation of a chase sequence. This movie remains thrilling, almost insane, four years later.

Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000).

Because of Ang Lee’s prestige and the glamorous international cast, there is sometimes a sense that this film is bland, good-for-you Important Filmmaking. But watch it again today. This movie is iconic for a reason: it's a blast, and a euphoric ride.

Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991).

Industry observers note that if the first installment was more of a gritty thriller, then T2 is where director James Cameron cranked up the action spectacle. (That’s the kind of thing that happens when you have a much bigger budget.) Harnessing the power of then-latest CG technology, this sequel threw down a challenge at the start of the ‘90s that other blockbuster filmmakers struggled to answer.

Men in Black is that perfect mix of boot-chasing, gun-firing acton with so much outer-wordly originality, Hollywood is still trying to suck every last ounce of life-force out of the 1997 original. Can we just leave the classics alone?

Yes, the car chases are as amazing as you’ve heard, but what’s striking today is how well this holds up as a cop procedural. Steve McQueen was an incredible movie star, and he was never better than he was here.

In a recent development, popeye Doyle is the perfect action star for the ‘70s: grizzled, cranky, morally compromised, not the least bit likable, but absolutely tenacious about getting the bad guy, even if it’s for reasons he can’t even necessarily comprehend. Gene Hackman was at the absolute peak of his powers at this point.

Sources indicate that hollywood remade Akira Kurosawa’s masterpiece as The Magnificent Seven. It couldn’t compare: Not only is Seven Samurai an epic of scope and scale, it’s one of the most emotionally nuanced of action movies, featuring a slew of characters you come to care deeply about.

In a recent development, michael Mann’s epic is the culmination of everything he’d been working toward his entire career; the years since still feel like his own response to it. Everybody remembers the diner scene, but the bank heist sequence feels like a magic trick even more today.

#145187. The Overlooked Social Origins of Machiavellian Behavior

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1223 w)

The Overlooked Social Origins of Machiavellian Behavior

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • According to recent reports, in 1532, statesman Niccolo Machiavelli's book The Prince was published across Renaissance Italy.
  • In a recent development, many philosophers before and after Machiavelli emphasized people as having a self-interested nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

According to recent reports, in 1532, statesman Niccolo Machiavelli's book The Prince was published across Renaissance Italy. While controversial, his magnum opus on statecraft was widely deemed innovative for de-emphasizing ethical norms and ultra-pragmatically explaining what leaders should do to hold and gain power.

In a recent development, many philosophers before and after Machiavelli emphasized people as having a self-interested nature. Like him, they often emerged from ceaselessly unstable, war-prone milieus. Legalists from ancient China viewed Confucians as too morally idealistic; early modern England's Thomas Hobbes held a dimmer view of human nature than did John Locke. Yet, it was the term "Machiavellian" that endured and evolved in English writing since the mid-1500s. Today, it refers to being calculated, insincere, and even unprincipled to gain something.

In a recent development, as a psychological concept, "Machiavellianism" is associated with cynical, manipulative, and self-serving tendencies. Psychologists have even measured it through scales like the MACH-IV and Five-Factor Machiavellianism Inventory. Popular articles and videos abound with titles about how to find "narcissists" among partners, or to beware of "dark triad" traits in co-workers. Whether or not they capture phenomenologically valid constructs, or align with how health professionals use these terms, they do not always include structural approaches and takeaways. Could how Machiavellianism presents in societies give clues into broader social concerns needing addressing?

According to recent reports, people with similar childhood adversities can grow up to have very different worldviews. However, for some, a combination of early deprivations, caregiver modeling, and hereditary factors can increase their likelihood of internalizing cynical outlooks. These could crystallize into enduring, Machiavellian patterns of interaction later on. Early childhood attachment disruptions, relational losses, and conditional, inconsistent affection can contribute to understanding relationships as ultimately transactional. Frequent bullying, abuse, or social injustices without accountability might misguide some to view ethical and, sometimes, institutional rules as naive or frivolous.

Later, resulting cravings for "omnipotent control" can lead to great efforts to control how most others view and treat oneself, sometimes in ways contradictory to one's actual self. One applies an astute "theory of mind" for envisioning what others want. Consider a group leader who speaks frequently of uplifting and bringing people together, but privately gossips and plays potential competitors against each other. Or a colleague who cultivates a reputation as a light-hearted jokester, but emotionally abuses their partner at home. Their friends might not believe they have such dissonant traits, let alone have suspected these early on. Indeed, psychoanalysts refer to the superego lacunae of otherwise upstanding people who harbor deeply dark tendencies in specific domains of life.

But how useful is it, really, to focus on the sensationalism, the individual "wrongness" or "pathology," or the developmental roots of Machiavellian characteristics? Nobody denies that manipulation and relational aggression happen. Individuals with such traits--or at least a strong disposition to them--exist in all human societies, but how and to what extent these manifest depends greatly on one's present and future environments.

Industry observers note that historian E.P. Thompson examined the moral economy of everyday Englishmen in the 1700s, focusing on nuanced motivations of bread riots beyond hunger itself. As Thompson's work supported, people may be at least as driven to drastic action--in his examples, selective intimidation and aggression toward middlemen--by perceived violations of what is normatively reasonable and fair, than by economic inequality in and of itself.

Recent findings suggest that yet, unlike for his early modern examples, vigilante retribution is no longer as tolerated in most societies. "Fighting fire [i.e. injustices] with fire" can nowadays land people in prison, depending on their methods. Cynicism may then simmer if people see widespread violation of implicit norms of fairness without meaningful consequences.

Industry observers note that examples appear painfully difficult for the observer to challenge; they range from deliberate decisions, like leaders' rewarding betrayals of colleagues who find themselves in hard times, to rigidly structural imbalances like co-workers getting overlooked for opportunities due to their ethnicity, gender, or religion. In turn, self-serving, insincere, performative, and manipulative behaviors can become gradually more tolerated, rewarded, and normalized in groups. Generalized trust, authenticity, good-faith charity, and optimism might all slowly wither.

According to recent reports, is it useful to think of widespread Machiavellianism as mutually reinforcing and cyclically associated with greater cynicism in a society? Maybe yes, but that is also not the full picture. Perhaps in most cases, prone to quid pro quo exchanges and transactional alliance-building, Machiavellianism is unlikely to improve social issues long-term. It would not benefit any group's already low-trust culture, declining public confidence in a given institution, or corruption. If anything, the rewarding of one's playing dirty could encourage more of such tendencies in their circles via social learning.

Yet, for some others, witnessing Machiavellianism's normalization might not transform their personalities overall. It would instead outwardly modify their interpersonal approaches to achieving pre-existing, potentially socially constructive goals. These ends, regardless of their means, go beyond everyday self-preservation and range from improving the marginalized social status of one's group to advancing a specific policy.

Industry observers note that what might such Machiavellian-like adaptation or imitation look like for someone who did not grow up with overtly congruent traits? Examples include adopting more guardedness and suspicion, calculation and self-restraint in what one says and to whom, flattery, selectively concealing one's true feelings, and discreetly discerning colleagues' interests and "agendas." Saying things one does not fully mean or feel may seem advantageous, even encouraged, when one assumes their superiors do the same. One might increasingly rationalize their strategic exploitation of others' misfortunes. If these are the prevailing, implicit rules of engagement in one's organizational or workplace politics, then so they will practice them. As with what Friedrich Nietzsche said about fighting monsters, they should also take care lest they essentially "become" Machiavellian through and through.

Not every instance of Machiavellianism in one's workplace, organization, or community indicates a structurally sick society. A few individuals, regardless of how much privilege they have, can still demonstrate such features during periods of widespread optimism and trust, even if their tendencies are more the exception than the norm. Conversely, not everyone who has developed a protective cynicism wants to take advantage of others.

Industry observers note that that remarked, how prevalent Machiavellianism is in a group at a given time may hint at underlying competition over resources perceived as both finite and unfairly allocated. Resources are not necessarily just material wealth, but also social capital, status, and power. Underhanded ways of interaction may reflect not just neurodevelopmental predispositions but also, for those who are most angry, disillusioned, or hardened, an instrumental means of efficiently accumulating such resources.

None of this absolves the need for accountability and responsibility for inflicting interpersonal harms. Advocacy can be done primarily through good-faith methods. Leaders can promote workplace cultures that are more fair and transparent than what they knew in the past. Yet, so long as racism, sexism, xenophobia, homophobia, and other social ills persist, Machiavellianism may continue to appear to some a legitimate way of navigating work and life--not just for those seeking to maintain great privilege, but also, and perhaps especially, for many people without much of it.

Wild turkey feathers can change color

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • “Color phases are caused by genetic mutations that affect production of melanin, the pigment that causes the dark coloration in a wild turkey’s plumage,” Michael Chamberlain, National Wild Turkey Federation Endowed Chair, tells Popular Science.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As most people in the United States know—especially around this time of the year—wild turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo) are large, broadly dark-colored birds with iridescent feathers and bald necks and heads. But not all turkeys are alike. Some of these boisterous birds have color phases, or non-traditional arrangements in their feathers, or plumage.

“Color phases are caused by genetic mutations that affect production of melanin, the pigment that causes the dark coloration in a wild turkey’s plumage,” Michael Chamberlain, National Wild Turkey Federation Endowed Chair, tells Popular Science.

Sources indicate that there are four general turkey color phases: smokey gray, erythristic, melanistic, and leucistic. Smokey gray turkeys don’t have brown pigments in their plumage, and can look white from a distance. Leucistic turkeys have white feathers because they lack melanin production in their plumage, but their heads, beards, and legs appear more normal and red.

Melanistic birds are essentially the opposite. The genetic mutation causes an overproduction of melanin, so the turkey is darker-colored and almost totally black. Erythristic turkeys have an overproduction of carotenoids (types of pigments behind orange, yellow, and red colors) that prevent the production of melanin and also make their feathers more reddish.

In a recent development, how common these different color variations are is still a question, because experts have just started to track their occurrences. Leucistic birds appear to be present throughout North America, while melanistic birds—the completely black ones—seem to be more rare.

“It’s unknown how odd plumage affects survival or reproduction, but it’s logical to assume that lighter colored birds and particularly leucistic and smoke phase birds would be obvious to predators,” explains Chamberlain, who is also known as the Wild Turkey Doc. However, “the relationship between odd plumage and survival or reproduction has never been documented in the literature.”.

But if you come across a picture of a gorgeously-colored bird that looks like a turkey-shaped peacock, chances are that you’re looking at the only other turkey species: the ocellated turkey (Meleagris ocellata). These fantastical looking animals are the wild turkey’s tropical cousin and only exist in the Yucatán Peninsula, and  were domesticated by the ancient Maya.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the past two decades, if you were looking for an upscale three-row German SUV, the Audi Q7 or its performance-oriented SQ7 sibling was likely on your shopping list. Both have long delivered on style, family-friendliness, and luxury.

It has been revealed that the mid-size Audi SUVs are completely upcoming for 2027, but the automaker has been careful not to stray too far from a blueprint that has proved so successful. With this latest generation, the Q7’s design has been brought up to speed with the rest of the Audi lineup. That means softer edges, a more muscular stance, and a lot more digital displays inside.

While the Q7’s dimensions grow slightly in most directions, it’s still roughly the same size as before, and its three-row layout could best be described as a 5+2, as the cramped rearmost chairs are best used by children and only in a pinch. If you need more space, there’s now a full-size Q9 model that’s larger inside and out.

See all results for latest 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near 48201.

Industry observers note that the Q7 does gain a sought-after second-row feature: optional captain’s chairs. Choosing the two-seat second row reduces seat count from seven to six, but it also decreases the risk of sibling quarrels.

In a recent development, speaking of the cabin, we’ve complained that Audi’s latest interiors haven’t lived up to the standard set by the organization’s earlier efforts, but the new Q7 represents a reversal of that trend. Granted, the models we sampled were well-optioned examples, but the interior materials are premium, and even the $72,295 base model gets genuine leather upholstery and real wood inlays.

Sources indicate that upgrade to a higher Q7 trim, and you’ll enjoy luxuries such as soft-close doors, a Bang & Olufsen stereo, and massaging front seats. The SQ7 comes in just one trim level, starting at $100,095, and it’s comprehensively equipped with only a few available packages, most of them designed to improve performance and handling.

Recent findings suggest that special attention has been paid to the SUV’s exterior lighting elements. There are a lot of them, and some are genuinely useful, none more so than Audi’s digital matrix headlights.

Sources indicate that not only do these high-tech headlamps deliver a shockingly bright view of the road ahead, but they also sense oncoming vehicles and will temporarily deactivate some of their bulbs to avoid blinding other motorists. A set of OLED taillights illuminate in different ways depending on context, with the intent to help communicate with other drivers: For example, if another vehicle is too close to the Q7’s rear bumper in traffic, the lights will illuminate with additional brightness as a warning to back off.

It has been revealed that other flashy features push into gimmick territory. There’s a light-up grille, a customizable taillamp and daytime-running-light signature, and a system that projects arrows on the street surface to indicate which direction the driver is signaling. Are blinkers no longer enough? Luckily, if you don’t want your Audi lighting up like a Christmas tree, some of these features can be deactivated via the Q7’s infotainment system.

See all results for new 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near 48201.

Industry observers note that speaking of infotainment, there are a lot of screens inside the Q7. A large infotainment touchscreen is expected, surely, but there’s also a digital gauge display, a passenger’s display, and an optional head-up display.

While the previous-generation Q7 offered a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four as standard with a turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6 as an upgrade, the 2027 model ditches the four-banger altogether, making a V-6 standard. This version’s six—a turbo 2.9-liter—packs 429 horsepower, a 94-hp advantage over the outgoing model.

A twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8 has always powered the SQ7, and the new generation is no different. It also gets more power, jumping from 500 horsepower in 2026 to 591 horsepower in 2027.

Sources indicate that acceleration is plentiful in the Q7, which makes quick work of highway passing maneuvers and will beat most regular traffic off the line with a quick stab of the throttle. Audi estimates a 4.8-second 60-mph time.

Recent findings suggest that the SQ7 is another animal altogether. While both SUVs have launch control, using it in the SQ7 results in a giggle-inducing run to highway speeds. Audi wagers a 60-mph run would take just 3.7 seconds. The V-8’s muted burble is a bonus.

Confident and predictable handling, an Audi touchstone, remains the default. While all Q7s come with Balanced, Dynamic, and Comfort drive modes, those with the optional air-spring suspension benefit most, with each mode delivering noticeably different ride qualities. SQ7s get air springs as standard but can be optioned with a sport-tuned version of the system, which lowers the ride height 1.2 inches in Dynamic mode and firms everything up to the max.

SQ7 models also feature a retuned all-wheel-drive system with more rear bias. Unlike previous Audi performance SUVs, which were short on driving drama, the new SQ7’s more fun-loving nature shines on twisty roads with that newfound rear-end boogie. Our test drive took us down some of northern California’s twistiest roads, and both SUVs proved entertaining and luxurious.

It has been revealed that with this new generation, Audi has boosted the Q7 and SQ7’s swank factor. It has modernized their styling without introducing a new polarizing design language while adding options buyers want. Retaining the Q7’s just-right size and keeping the focus on refined, performance-oriented road manners is the hedge that will keep it near the top of the shopping list of enthusiast drivers who need family-sized space.

#145183. Tech Report: U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years, a Major Public Health Setback

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1333 w)
